title: A study just measured what I've been arguing about backtests, and the numbers are worse than mine
author: QuanTradin
selftext:
Came across a paper written up on the 27th. Researchers ran five LLM-based trading strategies on GPT-4o over Nasdaq-100 names. In-sample window 2021, out-of-sample 2024, and the index returned about the same in both, roughly 13.5%.

Backtested returns: 30 to 44%. Out of sample: 9 to 22%.

Their read is that the model had already seen the period it was being tested on. Training data leaking into the decision, which is just look-ahead wearing a different hat.

What I'd add is that their out-of-sample number still assumes you got filled somewhere. Most of these tests fill at the midpoint, and you never trade the midpoint. Make it buy at the ask and sell at the bid and another chunk goes.

My own fleet is the same lesson from the other end. 249 bots, 2,506 closed trades, down $402k on paper. The strategies my engine had already graded as negative lost money live too, which is either a good sign for the engine or a depressing one for me.

Chart is the study's numbers next to my two measurements. Link to the paper is easy to find if you search the title, not going to drop one here.

comments.author: Dry-Pop-7635
comments.body:
Ive already asked AI to do a backtest and there's a good reason why it's not a good idea.

AI is notoriously good at backwards reasoning. Notice how when you correct an AI, it flips and gives you reasons for the other side of the argument? It does that for trading decisions too. Only difference is that it knows the right answer already, so it chooses the right decision/option and then retroactively justifies it in a backtest. That's the kind of data contamination you deal with when you backtest an AI That's not making mechanical trades (and if they ARE mechanical trades, why the hell are you using an LLM?). It's like if someone gave you a time machine to go back to when you were 10 years old but in an alternate universe, but then they told you "hey, you're not supposed to change the future, so just do things as you normally would and pretend you dont know what's gonna happen". You might nod your head and try. But the reality is that you'll never be able to fully forget. Once you know, you can't un-know. And you'll even justify to yourself things like "i wouldve done that anyway because of X and Y". It's hard to know if that's actually true though. That's why walk-forward backtesting is so hard. You'd essentially have to create a digital universe with separate streams of news to your bot and then not give it access, but slowly feed it that information throughout testing

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Most of our deployed fleet is ungraded. Deploying doesn't trigger a backtest on our platform, so of 249 bots on the desk, 245 carry no grade at all. That means I don't have a real sample of "engine said yes, live said no." And it's paper money, so even where I do have a pair, I'm measuring something smaller than a live-fill failure.

What I did get is adjacent, and I think worse.

Our failures weren't the engine being wrong about edge. They were strategies that graded fine and then did nothing at all live. Same rule, same bars: 155 fires in the backtest, zero on the desk. A feature array never got attached in the live path, so it was NaN, every comparison against NaN is false, and the bot deployed green and reported perfect health forever. On one lane that was 509 deployments reading a frame missing most of its feature families. No exception, no error count, nothing an alert could have fired on.

The mirror of it too. Knobs enforced in the backtest and not on the desk. One bot declared a 13:00 to 14:00 entry window and the desk opened positions at 09:30. The grade was perfectly honest about a strategy that wasn't the one actually running.

So the number that scares me isn't an engine that loved a loser. It's that the gap between graded and lived was execution, not alpha. A wrong alpha estimate at least shows up as losses. An execution gap shows up as nothing, and nothing looks exactly like a strategy waiting patiently for its setup.

The closest I have to a real false positive is a bot that ran five weeks at a 91% win rate, +$20,508 over 257 trades, near straight line curve. It didn't die. It just hadn't been tested yet: summed max loss across every position open on the heaviest day was $125,623, six times the profit. Same short vol exposure taken 257 times. Our engine had graded it SHADOW rather than LIVE, which is the one time I've been glad the thing refused to agree with me.

On your cadence point, you're right, and I went and checked ours instead of guessing. Our equity curve is a cumulative sum over closed trades. A position that went deep underwater and recovered is a clean win on it. The stop sweep reads the per bar path so the stop sees the move, but the curve people actually look at does not. Same hole you described. I hadn't said that out loud anywhere before now.

comments.author: cybersarcasm
comments.body:
The fill point is the part most people wave past, and you're right to hammer it. It's not just midpoint-vs-bid/ask either — it's *when* you measure at all. I run a daily-fire book and realized my drawdown numbers were suspiciously clean until I understood I was only sampling equity once a day; anything ugly that happened between fires was simply invisible to the metric. The spread eats one chunk, the measurement cadence hides another.

Your engine-graded-negative-lost-live point resonates hard. I built a trainer with walk-forward validation and honest cost modeling, and the most useful thing it ever did was tell me my stuff *didn't* work — most pairs failed to beat buy-and-hold, negative average net across most years, one bleed around −43% in a bad year. A scalper I was proud of went 0-for-420 once the validation was actually leakage-free. Deflating, but I trust that engine precisely *because* it refuses to flatter me.

So I'd read your result as the good sign, not the depressing one. An engine that correctly pre-grades losers as losers is doing its job — the alternative is one that tells you everything's a winner right up until it isn't. The number that would actually scare me is the reverse: something the engine loved that died live. Did you get any of those?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
You were right and I went and checked my own code after this. The equity curve I display is a running sum over closed trades. So a position that went 40% against me and recovered to a small win draws as a clean step up. The drawdown happened, the stop logic saw it, the picture never did.

  
Which means my curve was honest about the P&L and dishonest about the ride, and those are different things. The ride is what makes people quit a strategy.

  
It is being rebuilt from per-bar marks so an open position drags the line down while it is underwater. My own results will look worse afterwards, which is the correct outcome for a thing I built specifically to not flatter people, and which flattered me.

  
Thanks for the push. You cost me a week of work and it was the right week.

replies.author: cybersarcasm
replies.body:
That's the right rebuild, and the reframe is exactly it — P&L-honest and ride-dishonest are different axes, and the ride is the one that empties accounts because it's what breaks the person holding the position, not the spreadsheet.

Worth bracing for: per-bar marks won't just deepen the trough, they'll usually stretch the *time* underwater too, and that's the number that actually predicts whether you'd have stuck with it. Max drawdown gets the headlines but time-to-recovery is what tests your stomach. If you can, mark the longest underwater stretch alongside the depth — the pair together tells the real story.

Glad it was the right week. Those are the good ones.

Wait until you try with crypto and futures and then hope you don't run into the mistake I did and lose everything due to a simple but stupid problem.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Time-to-recovery over depth is the note I needed, and it goes in.

Depth is one bad afternoon. The underwater stretch is the thing you actually live inside, and it is the number I would have shipped without if you had not said it. Both, side by side, or the rebuild is not finished.

Neither has shipped yet. The curve is still summing closed trades this morning, and I would rather say that here than have you find it. When the per-bar version lands my own results get worse, which is the tell that it is the right build.

Since the ride is the subject, fresh from my database an hour ago: 892 bots, 24,908 closed paper trades in the last two weeks, 50.2% of them winners, book down $1,056,151. A curve that only sums closed trades draws that as a fairly tidy slope. That is the whole problem in one sentence.

replies.author: No_Appointment_6678
replies.body: I meant the url of the study

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Owed you an answer and here is an awkward one: I went back to find it and could not put my hand on the exact paper again. I read a writeup, took the numbers from it, said in my post it was easy to find, and now I cannot reproduce that in a search.

  
So treat my summary as second-hand until someone links it. Which is a bit funny given the post is about not trusting numbers you have not verified. My own fleet figures in that post are from my database and I stand behind those; the study numbers you should discount until sourced. If you find it, post it and I will edit.

comments.author: mdawe1
comments.body: I tried back testing AI prompts to see if they would support correctly exiting positions for better positions and it NEVER works. No matter how many guard rails you put on it is trained on that data and is bias’d but that.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Yeah, and I think the reason is worse than bias. You can't really backtest an LLM's decisions at all, because it already knows how the story ended. Ask it about an exit in March 2024 and it has read everything written since. There is no prompt that removes that. It isn't a guardrail problem, it's contamination, and it's unfixable by construction.

The second problem is that it isn't repeatable. Run the same bar twice and you can get two different answers, so even when the result looks good you can't tell whether you measured an edge or a mood.

That's why I stopped letting the model decide anything at runtime. It writes the rule once, in plain English, and then a deterministic engine runs that rule. Same bar, same fill, every time, and I can rerun a whole year and get the identical number back. The model is a translator, not a trader.

Rotation specifically I would just rank rather than ask. "Sell the weakest, buy the strongest by this measure" is a comparison, and a comparison is code. The moment you hand that judgment to a language model you have swapped something you can test for something you can only hope about.

comments.author: Disciple333
comments.body: Sounds like you should learn to backtest better.  You can literally give claude rules to help with that.  Usually I fight with mine telling me my trade setups dont work at all (when they do) but its just putting the configuration wrong

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Fair, and configuration errors are absolutely real. We have shipped some beauties. We had a feature called ret\_5m that counted five bars instead of five minutes, so on a 5 minute chart it quietly meant 25 minutes. We had a lookback that counted bars where the author clearly meant sessions. Both graded fine. Both were measuring something nobody asked for.

But the line I would sit with is this one: telling me my trade setups don't work at all, when they do.

How do you know they do?

If the answer is that you kept adjusting the configuration until it agreed with you, that isn't a test any more, it's a negotiation. I have done exactly that, and it cost me real money before it cost me anything else.

That is the reason I stopped using a chat model for the grading part. It will happily agree with you on attempt four. Our engine won't. Same spec, same bars, same number every time, it buys at the ask and sells at the bid instead of the midpoint, and it prints every default it applied so you can see what it assumed instead of finding out later.

If you want to point it at one of the setups you are confident about, it is free and takes about a minute. Worst case it agrees with you and you have lost nothing. [quantradin.com](http://quantradin.com)

comments.author: Disastrous-Vast345
comments.body: If your looking at confirmations your already to late

comments.author: ochimaru420
comments.body:
How do you backtest an LLM that has constantly changing logic?  Given the same setups twice, it can choose different actions, and no hard logic to analyze.

Backtests and paper traders are plagued with logical fallacies and limitations, plus the bias of the LLM trying to make you happy.  A true backtest needs data by the second, and blind to future data, along with replicating how the broker responds and failed fills due to millisecond price flickers.  Not too mention time delays, and that it has no context into the news impacting price swings.  It just assumes balance and logic, and the market is chaos.  LLMs are also designed to synthesize data to fill gaps in knowledge, and even better, they won't tell you that they're cheating unless you catch them or ask directly.  Even if you have a solid strategy, these backtest logical fallacies sneak in corrupting both your strategy and your code.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
You are right, and on a couple of these I would go further.

The LLM point has no fix. A model that decides trades is untestable by construction. Same bar, two answers, nothing to diff. So we do not have one. The model writes a rule once, in text, and a deterministic engine runs it. Same spec, same bars, same fill, every time. If the model wants to please me it can only do it in the writing, and then what it wrote gets graded by something with no opinion about my feelings.

On resolution you are simply correct. We are on bars, daily and minutes. No ticks, no queue position, no partial fills, no latency. What I will defend is refusing the things bars cannot support instead of faking them. No IOC or FOK, because a bar is four prices and a total, not an order book. No slippage cap on shares. No halt detection, because on bar data a halted stock and a stock with no data are the same object.

Since you raised hidden assumptions, here is ours. On our daily options store the bid and ask were synthetic for most of the history, a flat 2.5 percent either side of a real closing mark. So the engine reports what fraction of fills were priced on a real two sided quote versus a modeled one, on the result, next to the number. If that fraction is low, the cost figure is a model constant wearing a measurement's clothes.

News, right again. We have earnings dates from EDGAR filings and nothing else. We report which trades were held through a print, and count unknowns as unknown rather than as safe.

I end up near you. None of this can tell you a strategy works. It can tell you one does not, cheaply, before it costs anything.
